passage:
On the third night, Vikas and Salma were still in the small office above the hardware shop in town, sending emails. The one deck, unchanged, went to every investor address they could find, two hundred of them. Salma pasted names until the tea went cold.
The replies came fast and short. "Thanks, but we only back financial apps." "Not our area." "We don't invest at this stage." Some were kind, most were automatic.
By the end of the week they had spent long hours and had not one meeting. Vikas stared at the screen, thinking each no meant the idea was bad, when many just said the fund was the wrong one. Salma closed the laptop and said nothing.

qa.q: Where were Vikas and Salma sending the emails from?
qa.a: They sent them from the small office above the hardware shop in town.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling while reading the replies?
qa.a: Vikas was discouraged, taking each no as proof the idea was weak, which is why the screen was hard to look away from.

qa.q: What could Vikas and Salma try instead of another mass email?
qa.a: They could research a short list of investors who back businesses like theirs and write to each about why they fit.

qa.q: How might an investor see a deck sent to everyone?
qa.a: An investor sees a message that ignores their focus, so a quick no from a fund that backs something else is the natural reply.

grounding: The passage shows a founder sending the same deck to hundreds of investors without research, getting fast rejections and wasting the team's time.
